X-Wines: Predicting Wine Ratings¶

Research question: How much do historical ratings, wine attributes, and rating context contribute to predicting a later wine rating?

Historical ratings, wine attributes, and rating context are evaluated on a shared chronological split, with separate checks for unseen wines and recommendation ranking.

Prediction and study design · Related research · Data and exploration · Models and implementation · Evaluation and interpretation · Conclusions · Reproduction

def load(name, **kwargs):

    return pd.read_csv(REPORTS / name, **kwargs)

Prediction objective and study design¶

Given user $u$, wine $i$, and declared query context, predict the continuous rating $r_{ui}\in[1,5]$. User and wine identity, catalogue attributes, rating date, and rated vintage are possible inputs. Rating date and vintage must be known for context-aware predictions. We predict ratings conditional on an observed rating event, not purchases, sales, or satisfaction across all unobserved pairs.

The primary question is future-rating prediction. A global chronological split uses 120,000 training, 15,000 validation, and 15,000 test events. Timestamp ties stay together. Training fits every vocabulary, imputer, aggregate, and parameter; validation selects settings; test evaluates the selected configurations. Predictions are clipped to [1,5], without half-star rounding.

RMSE is primary because large rating errors receive a larger penalty. MAE gives a more direct typical absolute error in stars. Neither measures list quality, so ranking is a separate, secondary experiment. Global/user/item means, additive user–wine biases, and a linear model with the same features provide comparison points before attributing gains to model complexity.

Sensitivity protocols. Random splitting keeps repeated user–wine pairs together; it asks a different interpolation question. The disjoint-wine protocol puts complete wines in separate partitions and tests prediction without an item's rating history. It simulates missing history, not actual launch dates. The same saved membership hashes underpin the model notebooks. Scores across protocols do not share identical test distributions.

Related research and model choices¶

Dataset origin. de Azambuja, Morais and Filipe (2023), X-Wines introduce an open wine-rating dataset assembled from web sources in 2022. Their examples include neighbourhood recommendation and comparisons of recommender algorithms. We use the smaller Slim edition to compare identity, static attributes, and context under fixed partitions; our protocols and scores are not a direct replication of their published experiments.

Neighbourhood recommendation. Sarwar et al. (2001), Item-Based Collaborative Filtering Recommendation Algorithms motivate prediction from item similarities. Our implementation compares Jaccard, cosine and Pearson similarities and shrinks neighbour corrections toward an additive bias prediction. The resulting gain is small on this sample, so similarity alone does not explain the larger gains of context-aware models.

Latent factors. Koren, Bell and Volinsky (2009), Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems describe bias terms, regularized latent factors and extensions of collaborative filtering. Those ideas motivate our bias, ALS, SVD and SVD++ comparisons. Their success in other rating domains is motivation rather than evidence of a gain on Slim; our tuned factors do not clearly outperform the additive reference.

Sparse feature interactions. Rendle (2010), Factorization Machines describes factorized interactions among general sparse features, unifying several factorization models. We borrow the second-order prediction equation and efficient interaction calculation. Here, a matched linear model has almost the same test error as the FM, so additional interactions do not show a material point-estimate gain.

Temporal drift. Koren (2010), Collaborative Filtering with Temporal Dynamics models changing rating behaviour on Netflix. Our simpler year/month features are motivated by that concern, but are not timeSVD++. Their validation improvement agrees with the importance of drift; different datasets and protocols prevent a numerical comparison with Netflix results.

Similar review data. McAuley and Leskovec (2013), Hidden Factors and Hidden Topics study rating prediction with review text, including wine/CellarTracker data. Their text-informed factors can help sparse cases. These X-Wines CSVs do not expose the corresponding review text, so we examine structured attributes instead and cannot claim to reproduce the text-based method.

Strong references. Rendle, Zhang and Koren (2019), On the Difficulty of Evaluating Baselines show how careful baseline tuning can change apparent model advantages. This motivates comparing FM against a linear model with identical features and tuned regularization. Their results do not imply that simple models always win; our conclusion is limited to these experiments.

Dataset, collection and preprocessing¶

The authors collected and validated ratings from 2012–2021. Their Full edition reports 100,646 wines and about 21 million ratings; those are published counts, not a Full-edition experiment here. Slim is the measured study sample. User identifiers are anonymized; production country and region are wine attributes, not consumer locations. Prices and purchase/exposure records are unavailable.

The upstream Test edition is a small example dataset, distinct from our held-out test partitions. Catalogue attributes are a retrospective 2022 snapshot. A chronological split cannot establish that every attribute was available at each historical rating time.

Ratings, activity and sampling¶

Rating mass is concentrated above the midpoint and activity is uneven across users and wines. Review frequency describes the sampled rating process; it is not a direct measure of demand. Sparse histories motivate regularization and explicit fallbacks for unseen IDs.

The Red–White comparison averages within-user differences among users with at least two ratings of each type. It does not isolate a causal type effect. The later split-half analysis asks a different question: whether residual preferences repeat after accounting for user/wine biases. A positive mean type difference can coexist with weak residual preference stability.

Feature representation and data quality¶

IDs and origin/type fields are categorical. Grape blends use fractional multi-hot weights of 1/k. ABV is scaled and imputed using unique training wines. Non-vintage or invalid ages use a training median and a missing indicator. Rating month uses sine/cosine; rating year and vintage age have declared scales. Entire catalogue vintage lists are excluded because they can contain later availability information.

Every metadata join preserves rating rows or raises an error. Unknown categorical levels contribute no learned coefficient; known bias/content terms provide fallbacks. Body/Acidity are partly review-derived and appear only in a caveated sensitivity experiment. Prices are never imputed from unrelated sources.

Feature encoder (src/factorization_machines.py, FMEncoder.fit): the vocabularies, the ABV scaling and the median vintage age are all learned from training rows only.

def fit(self, frame):
    wines = frame.drop_duplicates('WineID')
    abv = pd.to_numeric(wines.ABV, errors='coerce') if 'ABV' in frame else pd.Series(dtype=float)
    self.abv_median = float(abv.median()) if abv.notna().any() else 0.
    self.abv_sd = float(abv.std()) if abv.notna().sum() > 1 and abv.std() > 0 else 1.
    age = _age(frame) if {'Date', 'Vintage'} <= set(frame) else np.array([np.nan])
    self.age_median = float(np.nanmedian(age)) if np.isfinite(age).any() else 0.
    names, fields = [], []
    for field, _, col, _ in self._entries(frame):
        new = pd.unique(col)
        names.extend(new); fields.extend([field] * len(new))
    order = pd.Index(names)
    keep = ~order.duplicated()
    self.columns = order[keep]
    self.column_field = np.array(fields, dtype=object)[keep]
    self.index = pd.Series(np.arange(len(self.columns)), index=self.columns)
    return self

Models, objectives and implementation¶

The progression tests whether complexity contributes beyond strong references:

  • Additive bias: $\hat r_{ui}=\mu+b_u+b_i$, squared loss with separate user/item L2 penalties; alternating closed-form updates.
  • Item-based CF: bias prediction plus a damped weighted mean of neighbours' training residuals. Similarity choice, neighbourhood size and damping are selected on validation.
  • Matrix factorization: $\mu+b_u+b_i+p_u^Tq_i$, with regularized squared loss. Our solver uses alternating ridge solves; Surprise SVD uses SGD; SVD++ includes an implicit-feedback component.
  • Linear content/context: a sparse encoded feature vector with L2 regularization; a matched linear reference has the same inputs as the FM.
  • Factorization machine: $w_0+\sum_jw_jx_j+\sum_{j<l}\langle v_j,v_l\rangle x_jx_l$. Full-batch L-BFGS optimizes squared error with separate linear/factor penalties. At k=0 it reduces to a linear model.

Regression matches the rating target and loss. Classification accuracy is not the same objective; a classification approach would need an explicitly ordered loss or conversion to a comparable expected rating. Pairwise implicit-feedback objectives answer the separate ranking question.

Bias model (src/collaborative_filtering.py, BiasBaseline.fit): alternating exact updates of the wine biases and the user biases; reg_user and reg_item shrink users and wines with few ratings towards zero.

def fit(self, train):
    users = train.UserID.to_numpy(); items = train.WineID.to_numpy()
    r = train.Rating.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    self.mu = float(r.mean())
    self.user_ids, u = np.unique(users, return_inverse=True)
    self.item_ids, i = np.unique(items, return_inverse=True)
    n_u = np.bincount(u, minlength=len(self.user_ids))
    n_i = np.bincount(i, minlength=len(self.item_ids))
    bu = np.zeros(len(self.user_ids)); bi = np.zeros(len(self.item_ids))
    for _ in range(self.n_iter):
        bi = np.bincount(i, r - self.mu - bu[u], len(bi)) / (self.reg_item + n_i)
        bu = np.bincount(u, r - self.mu - bi[i], len(bu)) / (self.reg_user + n_u)
    self.bu = pd.Series(bu, index=self.user_ids)
    self.bi = pd.Series(bi, index=self.item_ids)
    self.user_count = pd.Series(n_u, index=self.user_ids)
    self.item_count = pd.Series(n_i, index=self.item_ids)
    return self

Item-CF prediction (ItemCF.raw): start from the bias prediction, then add a damped, similarity-weighted average of the user's leftover errors on the most similar wines they rated.

def raw(self, frame):
    base = self.baseline.raw(frame)
    items = frame.WineID.map(self.item_index).to_numpy()
    out = base.copy()
    self.neighbour_rows = 0
    for row, (user, item) in enumerate(zip(frame.UserID.to_numpy(), items)):
        if np.isnan(item) or user not in self.history:
            continue
        js, res = self.history[user]
        s = self.sim[int(item), js]
        keep = s > 0
        if not keep.any():
            continue
        s, res = s[keep], res[keep]
        if len(s) > self.k:
            top = np.argpartition(-s, self.k)[:self.k]
            s, res = s[top], res[top]
        out[row] += s @ res / (s.sum() + self.damping)
        self.neighbour_rows += 1
    return out

Sparse latent factors and feature interactions¶

ALS solves one regularized least-squares block at a time. The FM calculates all second-order interactions using sparse matrix products instead of enumerating every pair. Both require regularization: adding dimensions can reduce training error without improving validation. User/item factors can collapse toward the additive model when penalized strongly.

ALS update (ALSMF._solve): with the other side fixed, each user's (or wine's) bias and factor vector is an exact ridge regression.

@staticmethod
def _solve(groups, other_bias, other_vec, reg, reg_bias):
    """For each row group: ridge of target - other_bias on [1, other_vec]."""
    k = other_vec.shape[1]
    penalty = np.diag([reg_bias] + [reg] * k)
    bias = np.zeros(len(groups)); vec = np.zeros((len(groups), k))
    for g, (idx, y) in enumerate(groups):
        x = np.hstack([np.ones((len(idx), 1)), other_vec[idx]])
        w = np.linalg.solve(x.T @ x + penalty, x.T @ (y - other_bias[idx]))
        bias[g], vec[g] = w[0], w[1:]
    return bias, vec

FM prediction (src/factorization_machines.py, FactorizationMachine._raw): a linear term plus all pairwise feature interactions, computed with the identity $\tfrac12[(xV)^2 - x^2V^2]$ instead of looping over pairs.

def _raw(self, x, x2, w0, w, v):
    out = w0 + x @ w
    if self.n_factors:
        xv = x @ v
        out = out + 0.5 * ((xv ** 2).sum(1) - (x2 @ (v ** 2)).sum(1))
    return out

Validation selection and optimization¶

All displayed settings are from saved validation experiments. The main comparisons fit training only after selection, preserving the shared history cutoff. Different model families have different search budgets; a coarse ridge grid versus finer FM linear penalties is a potential explanation for small differences. A library Bayesian FM is an additional comparison, not the selected primary model.

The weakly regularized run illustrates overfitting; the selected run is judged by validation, not by its lower training error. Sparse encodings avoid materializing a dense user–wine matrix. Item CF still uses a dense wine similarity matrix on Slim; extending that implementation to the Full catalogue requires a sparse neighbour index. Reported Slim scaling measurements and Full projections are distinct: Full was not trained in this study.

Modeling trade-offs¶

Model What it learns Fit time on Slim Advantages Disadvantages
Additive bias $\mu$, one offset per user and per wine 0.08 s Exact closed-form updates; robust for users with few ratings No personalization beyond rating generosity and wine quality
Item CF wine × wine similarity (1,000 × 1,000) 2.2 s Interpretable ("similar to wines you rated"); no iterative training Similarity matrix grows with wines²; needs damping; prediction loops over rows
ALS MF $k$-dimensional user and wine vectors 11.4 s ($k$ = 16) Each step is an exact ridge solve: no learning rate, error falls monotonically Per-user Python loop; overfits unless λ ≥ 11; by λ = 20 the factors are zero and it equals the bias model
Surprise SVD / SVD++ same, plus implicit-feedback vectors 2.5 s ($k$ = 16) Fast compiled SGD; SVD++ adds which wines a user chose to rate One regularization for biases and factors; learning rate and epochs must be tuned
Linear on features ($k$ = 0) one weight per ID, attribute and context feature 2.5 s As accurate as the FM here; weights are directly readable No interactions between features
Factorization machine weight + factor vector per feature 19.5 s IDs, attributes and context in one model; scores unseen wines More hyperparameters; interactions overfit the 101 cold-start validation wines

Fit times are single measurements on one laptop (collaborative-filtering models) and from a separate run (linear/FM). They indicate relative cost, not a controlled benchmark.

Implementation challenges¶

  • fastFM does not build on Python 3.11 / NumPy 2, so the factorization machine is our own sparse L-BFGS implementation, with the myFM library as a Bayesian cross-check.
  • The textbook item-CF average made predictions worse: validation RMSE 0.4938 versus 0.4505 for the bias model. Averaging a user's residuals over a few neighbours adds noise; a damping term in the denominator fixes it (0.4496 with damping 1).
  • Surprise learns biases slowly by SGD with one shared regularization, so with standard settings its MF underfits the biases. Our ALS learns biases and factors exactly, with separate user and wine bias penalties, so "do latent factors help?" is a fair comparison.
  • A shared bias penalty in ALS first prevented strongly regularized ALS from reducing to the bias model. The validation grid exposed it (strongly regularized ALS stayed worse than the bias model); separate user and wine penalties fixed it.
  • Memory: a dense user × wine matrix is never built; ratings, similarities and features use sparse matrices.

Collaborative-filtering tuning and overfitting¶

Weak regularization drives training error far below validation error (overfitting); strong regularization shrinks the latent factors to zero, giving exactly the bias model. Code walkthrough: item similarity and SVD++¶

Jaccard, cosine and Pearson similarity between all pairs of wines at once, from sparse matrix products (B = who rated what, R = ratings, n = co-rating counts). Pearson uses co-rating users only; shrink distrusts pairs with few shared raters (src/collaborative_filtering.py):

    if kind == 'jaccard':
        size = np.diag(n)
        union = size[:, None] + size[None, :] - n
        sim = np.divide(n, union, out=np.zeros_like(n), where=union > 0)
    elif kind == 'cosine':
        dot = (R.T @ R).toarray()
        norm = np.sqrt(np.diag(dot))
        denom = norm[:, None] * norm[None, :]
        sim = np.divide(dot, denom, out=np.zeros_like(dot), where=denom > 0)
    else:
        sx = (R.T @ B).toarray()            # sum of x_i over users who rated i and j
        sxy = (R.T @ R).toarray()
        sxx = (R.multiply(R).T @ B).toarray()
        safe = np.where(n > 0, n, 1)
        cov = sxy - sx * sx.T / safe
        var = sxx - sx ** 2 / safe
        denom = np.sqrt(np.clip(var * var.T, 0, None))
        sim = np.divide(cov, denom, out=np.zeros_like(cov), where=(denom > 1e-12) & (n >= 2))
    if shrink:
        sim = sim * n / (n + shrink)
    np.fill_diagonal(sim, 0.)

Surprise SVD / SVD++ wrapper: the library fits by SGD; predictions are then vectorized from the learned parameters, and for SVD++ each user vector includes the implicit-feedback term $|N(u)|^{-1/2}\sum_{j \in N(u)} y_j$:

    def fit(self, train):
        from surprise import SVD, SVDpp, Dataset, Reader
        data = Dataset.load_from_df(train[['UserID', 'WineID', 'Rating']], Reader(rating_scale=(1, 5)))
        self.trainset = trainset = data.build_full_trainset()
        cls = SVD if self.algo == 'svd' else SVDpp
        kwargs = dict(n_factors=self.n_factors, n_epochs=self.n_epochs, lr_all=self.lr,
                      reg_all=self.reg, random_state=self.seed)
        if self.algo == 'svdpp':
            kwargs['cache_ratings'] = True
        start = time.perf_counter()
        self.model = cls(**kwargs).fit(trainset)
        self.fit_seconds = time.perf_counter() - start
        self.mu = trainset.global_mean
        self.user_index = pd.Series({trainset.to_raw_uid(x): x for x in trainset.all_users()})
        self.item_index = pd.Series({trainset.to_raw_iid(x): x for x in trainset.all_items()})
        m = self.model
        self.bu, self.bi, self.pu, self.qi = m.bu, m.bi, m.pu, m.qi
        if self.algo == 'svdpp':
            implicit = np.zeros_like(self.pu)
            for u in trainset.all_users():
                js = [j for j, _ in trainset.ur[u]]
                implicit[u] = m.yj[js].sum(axis=0) / np.sqrt(len(js))
            self.user_vector = self.pu + implicit
        else:
            self.user_vector = self.pu

Evaluation protocol and prediction validity¶

Event IDs, not row order, align predictions and labels. The shared scorer rejects missing/extra/duplicate IDs and non-finite scores, applies clipping, and reports RMSE/MAE. Published input and split hashes are immutable references; a rerun cannot silently redefine the benchmark.

The primary uncertainty analysis resamples users in a paired bootstrap, keeping both models' predictions aligned. These intervals condition on the fitted models and fixed split. Shared wines, retraining variation and time shifts are not fully captured. For the disjoint-wine experiment, user-bootstrap intervals do not measure uncertainty over newly sampled wines. Existing inspected test results remain exploratory if they influence further model choices.

Splits (src/experiments.py, make_splits): chronological 80/10/10 by time (rating-time ties stay together), random by user–wine pair, and cold-item by disjoint sets of wines.

def make_splits(ratings, protocol, seed=SEED):
    """Partition without labels; chronology never splits timestamp ties."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    if protocol == 'chronological':
        ordered = ratings.sort_values(['Date','RatingID'])
        t1 = ordered.Date.iloc[int(.8 * len(ordered))]
        t2 = ordered.Date.iloc[int(.9 * len(ordered))]
        part = np.where(ratings.Date < t1, 'train',
                        np.where(ratings.Date < t2, 'validation', 'test'))
    elif protocol == 'random':
        # Keep repeated user-wine events together if running on Full later.
        keys = ratings[['UserID','WineID']].drop_duplicates().sort_values(['UserID','WineID'])
        keys = keys.iloc[rng.permutation(len(keys))].copy()
        keys['partition'] = (['train'] * int(.8*len(keys)) +
                             ['validation'] * (int(.9*len(keys))-int(.8*len(keys))) +
                             ['test'] * (len(keys)-int(.9*len(keys))))
        assigned = ratings.merge(keys, on=['UserID','WineID'], validate='many_to_one')
        part = ratings.RatingID.map(assigned.set_index('RatingID').partition).to_numpy()
    elif protocol == 'cold_item':
        ids = np.sort(ratings.WineID.unique())
        ids = ids[rng.permutation(len(ids))]
        a, b = int(.8*len(ids)), int(.9*len(ids))
        part = np.where(ratings.WineID.isin(ids[:a]), 'train',
                        np.where(ratings.WineID.isin(ids[a:b]), 'validation', 'test'))
    else:
        raise ValueError(protocol)
    splits = {p: ratings.loc[part == p].copy() for p in ['train','validation','test']}
    validate_splits(splits, protocol, ratings)
    return splits

Scorer (src/pipeline.py, score_predictions): predictions are matched to test ratings by RatingID; missing, extra, duplicate or non-finite predictions are rejected, then predictions are clipped to [1, 5].

def score_predictions(reference, predictions):
    """Align by RatingID, require full coverage, then apply the shared clipping rule."""
    for frame, required in [(reference, ['RatingID', 'Rating']),
                            (predictions, ['RatingID', 'prediction'])]:
        if not set(required).issubset(frame.columns):
            raise ValueError(f'Required columns: {required}')
        if frame.RatingID.isna().any() or not frame.RatingID.is_unique:
            raise ValueError('RatingID must be non-null and unique')
    if set(reference.RatingID) != set(predictions.RatingID):
        raise ValueError('Prediction IDs must exactly match the evaluation partition')
    aligned = reference[['RatingID', 'Rating']].merge(
        predictions[['RatingID', 'prediction']], on='RatingID', validate='one_to_one')
    values = aligned.prediction.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    if not np.isfinite(values).all():
        raise ValueError('Predictions must be finite; missing scores cannot be dropped')
    return dict(rows=len(aligned), clipped=int(((values < 1) | (values > 5)).sum()),
                **metrics(aligned.Rating, np.clip(values, 1, 5)))

Paired user bootstrap (src/experiments.py, cluster_bootstrap): resample whole users 2,000 times and recompute the RMSE difference between two models on the same rows.

def cluster_bootstrap(frame, reference, candidate, n_boot=2000, seed=SEED):
    """Paired user-cluster bootstrap for micro-RMSE difference; negative favors candidate."""
    errors = pd.DataFrame({'u':frame.UserID.to_numpy(),
                           'ref':(frame.Rating.to_numpy()-reference)**2,
                           'new':(frame.Rating.to_numpy()-candidate)**2})
    by = errors.groupby('u').agg(ref=('ref','sum'),new=('new','sum'),n=('ref','size')).to_numpy()
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    samples = np.empty(n_boot)
    for b in range(n_boot):
        totals = by[rng.integers(0,len(by),len(by))].sum(axis=0)
        samples[b] = np.sqrt(totals[1]/totals[2])-np.sqrt(totals[0]/totals[2])
    return {'delta_rmse': metrics(frame.Rating,candidate)['rmse']-metrics(frame.Rating,reference)['rmse'],
            'ci_low':float(np.quantile(samples,.025)), 'ci_high':float(np.quantile(samples,.975)),
            'clusters':len(by), 'bootstrap_replicates':n_boot}

# Paired 95% bootstrap intervals for the change in test RMSE (negative = the model beats its reference).
def plot_intervals(axis, frame, delta, low, high, title):
    """Dot = change in test RMSE, line = 95% interval, one row per model."""
    positions = list(range(len(frame)))
    axis.hlines(positions, frame[low], frame[high], color=WINE)
    axis.plot(frame[delta], positions, 'o', color=WINE)
    axis.axvline(0, color=GRAY, linewidth=1)
    axis.ticklabel_format(axis='x', style='plain', useOffset=False)
    axis.locator_params(axis='x', nbins=4)
    axis.set(yticks=positions, yticklabels=frame['model'], title=title,
             xlabel='change in test RMSE (stars; negative = better)')

Unseen wines and activity groups¶

The chronological test contains only 16 events for wines without training history, so it is insufficient for a strong cold-item conclusion. The separate disjoint-wine test contains 14,536 events across 101 held-out wines. Its FM wins on validation but underperforms its ridge reference on test. We keep that failure, without using test to reselect a winner. Metadata is useful for scoring an unseen item, but larger interaction models do not automatically generalize to new wines.

Parameter interpretation¶

Coefficients describe conditional associations in a regularized, correlated feature representation. They are not causal effects or intrinsic wine quality. User/wine identity can absorb much of an attribute's signal; scale matters when reading numeric coefficients.

Country and grape weights (factorization machine)¶

The five highest and five lowest weights for categories with at least 5 training wines. Because the wine ID absorbs most of each wine's quality, these weights are shrunk towards zero. Adding the extra catalogue features (Body, Acidity and food pairings) changes validation RMSE by less than 0.0001, so they do not help on rated wines.

def top_and_bottom(field, n=5):
    """Highest and lowest FM weights for one metadata field (categories with at least 5 training wines)."""
    rows = weights[(weights['field'] == field) & (weights['train_wines'] >= 5)]
    rows = rows.sort_values('weight', ascending=False)
    return pd.concat([rows.head(n), rows.tail(n)])[['label', 'train_wines', 'weight']]

Collaborative-filtering parameters¶

$b_i$ is how much higher or lower a wine is rated than average after accounting for who rated it (wines with at least 30 training ratings). The top are iconic wines: Penfolds Grange, Dom Pérignon Oenothèque, and the two Pauillac first growths, Château Lafite Rothschild (564 ratings) and Château Mouton Rothschild (820). The bottom are inexpensive varietals and Retsina. In the same run, user biases $b_u$ had a standard deviation of 0.20 stars (90% of users between −0.34 and +0.28), and wine bias was almost unrelated to how often a wine is rated (Spearman 0.08).

Do the latent factors find taste groups?¶

For a less regularized ALS model ($k$ = 16, λ = 9, factors clearly non-zero) we checked how often a wine's 10 nearest neighbours in factor space share its type or country, compared with random neighbours. The factors barely group wines by type and only slightly by country, and the PCA projection shows no type clusters.

Is personal taste stable?¶

The table below tests whether users have repeatable personal preferences. For 1,536 users with at least 4 Red and 4 White training ratings, each user's Red-minus-White residual (after removing user and wine biases) is measured on two random halves of their ratings. The correlation between halves is only r = 0.03 (range -0.02 to 0.08 over 20 splits). Users differ in how generously they rate and wines differ in quality, but there is little repeatable "this user likes this kind of wine" signal. This is consistent with latent factors adding almost nothing over the bias model, although it does not prove that personal preferences are absent.

Ranking and recommendation diversity¶

Ranking is secondary to predicting observed ratings. The saved experiment uses 4,684 training-seen users with at least one eligible held-out rating of at least four stars, a 1,007-wine catalogue, and excludes each user's training wines. Unobserved wines are unlabeled; treating them as non-relevant introduces exposure/selection bias. Catalogue availability at each historical query time is unknown.

The ranked FM uses static features, because a never-rated candidate has no known rated vintage. It is not the context-aware model from the main rating table. Popularity has higher reported Recall@10 here; this does not mean it best predicts rating values or necessarily wins in an online experiment.

Conclusions and limitations¶

  • Strong additive references explain much of the predictable signal. Item CF adds a small gain; the tested latent-factor models do not clearly outperform the bias model.
  • Rating context accounts for more validation improvement than static attributes on warm wines. The calendar/age ablation identifies calendar time as the larger component in this experiment.
  • The matched linear model and FM have nearly equal test RMSE. Small gains over the original ridge can reflect regularization and search effort, not just interactions.
  • Unseen-item prediction and ranking remain harder questions. The cold-item FM fails to retain its validation advantage, and the ranking objective rewards a different behaviour from predicting rating values.
  • Conclusions are limited to the sampled catalogue, observed rating events, fixed partitions and tested searches. Retrospective metadata, user/item dependence, rating selection and missing historical availability limit causal and deployment claims.

This evidence connects the literature to the experiments: item similarity remains a useful small correction; factorized interactions are flexible but need not outperform a well-tuned linear reference; temporal drift deserves explicit modeling. The next experiment should preserve an untouched holdout and focus on the intended recommendation setting before increasing model complexity.

Data provenance and reproducibility¶

Every table and chart in this notebook is read from the saved results in reports/ (three figures come from reports/figures/); no model is trained here. The results were produced by the experiment notebooks generated by scripts/build_rating_analysis.py, scripts/build_collaborative_filtering.py and scripts/build_factorization_machines.py, using the code in src/. Data preparation, dependencies and the commands to re-run the experiments are in the repository README. Numerical results and run times can vary slightly with hardware and native libraries.

Repository: https://github.com/AviGon/Wine_Recommendation_System
